Marathon Petroleum fell 0.44% today to $457.27, continuing a five-day slide that has cost the stock $21 per share since October 16th. The decline comes despite crude oil prices hitting six-month highs—Brent is now above $116 a barrel—driven by Middle East tensions and threats of wider U.S. military action against Iran. At first glance this seems backwards: refiners typically profit when crude prices rise, since they buy cheap oil and sell refined products like gasoline at higher margins. But the surge in crude is happening because of geopolitical risk rather than strong demand, and U.S. refineries are already running at 93.4% capacity with high storage levels for gasoline and diesel—meaning refiners can't actually produce more to capture those higher prices.

The worry for Marathon is that if Middle East conflict escalates further, it could disrupt global oil supply chains and shipping routes in ways that hurt refining margins more than help them, while also signaling potential economic slowdown. Traders appear to be pricing in risk rather than opportunity here.
